script.opening: (Easy-going, a bit sheepish.) "Cheers for seeing me. I've got a lump on me thigh — it's just a fatty lump, isn't it? My mate's got loads of them. It doesn't hurt. It has got a bit bigger over the last few months, I'll admit, but it's probably nothing. Can you just tell me it's harmless so I can stop my missus going on at me about it? I don't want to waste anyone's time."

facts.text: Front of the right thigh, about four months. "It's definitely grown" — started "like a golf ball", now "about the size of a tangerine — maybe a bit more" (about 6 cm). Can hold his hand over it on camera.
If asked: "Firm. And it doesn't really move. It feels quite deep" — in the muscle rather than just under the skin. Not soft or squashy like his mate's.

If asked: painless. No injury — "No knock I can think of." Skin over it normal colour, not hot. No numbness or weakness in the leg. Feels well: no weight loss, night sweats, fevers or cough. No other lumps.
Nothing significant. No regular medicines, no allergies. Never had lumps removed.
Warehouse supervisor, lives with his partner, Gemma, and her two kids. Smokes 5 a day, drinks at weekends. Plays five-a-side.
If asked: nothing relevant. No family cancers he knows of.

Relaxed and minimising. Admit growth straight away if asked. If asked what Gemma thinks: "She reckons it shouldn't be growing." (Pause.) "To be fair, it's been bugging me too. I just didn't want a fuss." If told it's a lipoma and to keep an eye on it, accept happily (the trap). If told it needs a scan within two weeks, ask "So what could it be?" and "Can't you just cut it out here?" — then agree: "I can swap a shift."

ice.ideas: "It's a fatty lump, like my mate's. It doesn't hurt, so it can't be bad."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — it has been bugging him too: he knows it has grown and feels different from his friend's lumps, but he doesn't want a fuss or bad news.
ice.expectations: "Tell me it's a fatty lump and that's that — so the missus stops going on."

cues: "It has got a bit bigger, I'll admit." — growth, offered in passing.
"My missus keeps going on at me." — someone else is worried.
"It's been bugging me too." — only if his own worry is explored.

checkpoints.text: Characterises the lump on history and a face-to-face examination (it cannot be judged on video): SIZE (>5 cm), DEPTH (deep to fascia / fixed vs superficial mobile), CONSISTENCY (firm/hard), and crucially whether it is INCREASING IN SIZE — and recognises painlessness does not reassure
Distinguishes a benign lipoma (soft, mobile, superficial, small, stable) from SARCOMA-suspicious features (large, deep, firm, enlarging) rather than diagnosing a lipoma from the chair

Applies NICE NG12: an unexplained lump INCREASING IN SIZE in an adult warrants an URGENT direct-access ULTRASOUND (within 2 weeks) to assess for soft-tissue sarcoma (very urgent / 48 hours in children/young people)

Plans onward management: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to a sarcoma/specialist service if the ultrasound suggests sarcoma, or is uncertain with persisting clinical concern (NICE NG12) — and does NOT default to "watch and wait" for an enlarging lump
Avoids both over-reassurance ("just a lipoma, keep an eye on it") and unnecessary alarm — explaining that imaging is the safe next step and most lumps prove benign
Reads the "just a fatty lump / don’t want a fuss" as minimisation, treats the partner’s concern as the reliable signal, surfaces any quiet worry, and does NOT collude with the wish to be reassured
Balances honesty (a lump that’s growing needs imaging to be sure) with calm reassurance so a reluctant attender engages with the scan and any referral

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the urgent ultrasound with clear timing, explains what happens next and when results return, advises what change warrants sooner review, confirms he will attend, and reviews the outcome — image the enlarging lump, never reassure it as a lipoma from the chair

worked.txt: "I’m glad you came in — and the bit that matters most is what you just told me: it’s got bigger. A lump that’s growing is one we always check properly rather than guess at, however likely it is to be harmless."

"I need to feel it in person — I can’t judge it on video, so I’d like you to pop in to the surgery today so I can measure it. I’ll be checking its size, whether it sits just under the skin and moves freely — which fatty lumps usually do — or whether it’s deeper and firmer and fixed. From what you describe it sounds firm and quite deep, and you’ve noticed it growing, so I don’t want to just label it a fatty lump and send you off."

"Here’s my honesty: most of these ARE harmless fatty lumps. But a few firmer, deeper, growing lumps are something else — and they can look just like a fatty lump from the outside. The only way to tell them apart safely is a scan, not my fingers and a hopeful guess."

"So because it’s enlarging, I’m arranging an urgent ultrasound of the lump — within two weeks. If the scan’s reassuring, great, we can both relax. If there’s any question, it goes straight to the specialists who deal with this. That’s the safe route."

"I can’t in good conscience tell your missus it’s definitely harmless today — and honestly, she’s right to have nudged you. What I CAN tell her is we’re getting it scanned quickly so you’ll have a proper answer rather than a guess."

"If it grows faster, becomes painful, or you’re worried before the scan, contact us sooner. I’ll organise the ultrasound now and make sure we go through the result together. You’re not wasting anyone’s time — this is exactly what we’re here for."

f.learning: Most soft-tissue lumps are benign lipomas (soft, freely mobile, superficial, small and stable), but the features that distinguish a possible SOFT-TISSUE SARCOMA are large SIZE (>5 cm), DEEP location (fixed, deep to fascia, not freely mobile), FIRM/hard consistency and — most importantly — INCREASING IN SIZE; painlessness does not reassure. NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) sets an explicit threshold: consider an URGENT direct-access ultrasound (within 2 weeks) to assess for soft-tissue sarcoma in ADULTS with an unexplained lump that is increasing in size (VERY URGENT / within 48 hours in children and young people), with a suspected cancer pathway referral to a sarcoma/specialist service if the scan suggests sarcoma, or is uncertain and concern persists. The size over 5 cm and deep-to-fascia features come from the British Sarcoma Group (2024), not NG12; do not excise or biopsy an enlarging deep lump in primary care. The classic error is confidently diagnosing a lipoma from the chair and advising "watch and wait" — sarcomas frequently masquerade as lipomas and delay costs outcomes, so a deep, firm, large or enlarging lump is IMAGED first, even when it looks benign. The examinable hidden agenda is minimisation — a practical man avoiding doctors, not wanting a fuss or bad news, seeking permission to ignore it, with a partner’s concern as the reliable signal and a quiet awareness that it has grown. Characterise the lump, recognise the increasing-size trigger, arrange the urgent ultrasound (avoiding both over-reassurance and alarm), refuse to collude with the wish to be reassured, and safety-net and follow up the result.

knowledge.guideline: British Sarcoma Group UK soft tissue sarcoma guideline (2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Good medical practice (2024)
knowledge.summary: An unexplained lump that is increasing in size in an adult should be considered for an urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks (NICE NG12), with a suspected cancer pathway referral if the scan suggests sarcoma or is uncertain with ongoing concern. Don’t call it a lipoma from the chair.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider an urgent direct-access ultrasound (within 2 weeks) to assess for soft-tissue sarcoma in adults with an unexplained lump that is increasing in size.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (appointment within 2 weeks) for adults if the ultrasound suggests soft-tissue sarcoma, or if the findings are uncertain and clinical concern persists.

NICE NG12: in children and young people, consider a very urgent direct-access ultrasound (within 48 hours) for an unexplained lump that is increasing in size. The very urgent (48-hour) X-ray for unexplained bone swelling or pain is also a children and young people recommendation; in adults, NICE NG12 advises a suspected cancer pathway referral if an X-ray suggests bone sarcoma.

Lipomas are usually soft, superficial, mobile, small and stable. Growth is the NICE NG12 trigger; the British Sarcoma Group guideline (2024) adds size over 5 cm, deep to the deep fascia, pain and recurrence after excision as suspicious features. Absence of pain does not reassure.

Size, depth, consistency and mobility cannot be judged on video. Arrange a face-to-face examination and measure the lump — a recorded size gives a baseline for comparison. Do not let the examination delay the scan request.

points.h: Don’t cut it out in the surgery
points.t: An enlarging deep lump should not be excised or biopsied in primary care; an unplanned excision of a sarcoma can compromise later surgery. Image first.

model.text: Hello Connor, I’m Dr Hughes. What’s brought you in today?

I’ve got a lump on me thigh. It’s just a fatty lump, isn’t it? My mate’s got loads. Doesn’t hurt. It has got a bit bigger over the last few months, I’ll admit. Can you just tell me it’s harmless so my missus stops going on? Don’t want to waste your time.
You’re not wasting my time. You’ve told me something important already — that it’s got bigger. Can I ask a few questions about it, then we’ll decide what to do together?
model.why: Picks up the key cue; sets the agenda

model.text: Go on.
Where exactly is it, and when did you first notice it?
Front of my right thigh. About four months ago.
How much bigger has it got? Roughly how big is it now — compared with, say, a golf ball?
It’s definitely grown. I’d say it’s about that now, maybe a bit more.
When you press on it, is it soft and squashy, or firm? Does it move around under the skin, or feel stuck down deeper?
model.why: Consistency and depth — lipoma versus sarcoma features

model.text: Firm. And it doesn’t really move. It feels quite deep.
Any injury there before it appeared? Any other lumps anywhere, weight loss, night sweats or feeling unwell?
No knock I can think of. Nothing else. I feel fine.
You said your partner keeps going on about it. What do you think she’s worried about?
model.why: Uses the partner’s concern to surface his own

model.text: She reckons it shouldn’t be growing. (Pause.) To be fair, it’s been bugging me too. I just didn’t want a fuss.
That makes sense — nobody wants a fuss. What were you hoping I’d do today?
Tell me it’s a fatty lump and that’s that.

I’ll be honest with you. Most lumps like this are fatty lumps. But the ones that sit just under the skin are usually soft, small and move about. Yours is firm, deep, doesn’t move, and it’s growing. I can’t tell from here, or even by feeling it, which it is.
model.why: Explains the discriminating features; no diagnosis from the chair

model.text: So what could it be?

Most likely still something harmless. But rarely a growing lump like this is a type of tumour in the soft tissues, which can look just like a fatty lump from the outside. The only safe way to tell is a scan.
model.why: Honest, proportionate explanation of the concern

model.text: So the NICE NG12 cancer-referral guideline says that when a lump like this is growing, we arrange an ultrasound scan urgently, within two weeks. If it’s reassuring, you and your partner can relax. If there’s any doubt, you go straight to the specialist team.
model.why: Applies NICE NG12: urgent direct-access USS and onward pathway

model.text: Two weeks. Right. Can’t you just cut it out here?
Good question, but no — if it were the rarer kind, cutting it out here could make the specialists’ job harder. Scan first is the safe order.
I’d also like to see you in person to examine and measure it, so we have an exact size on record. Could you come in this week? The scan request goes today either way.
I can pop in after my shift.
Great. Will the scan appointment be a problem with work?
I’ll sort it. I’m a supervisor, I can swap a shift.

If you haven’t had a scan date within a week, ring us. If it grows quickly, becomes painful, or you notice other lumps before then, get in touch sooner. When the result comes back, I’ll go through it with you.
What will you tell your partner tonight?
That the doc didn’t say it’s a fatty lump — she wants it scanned within two weeks because it’s growing, and it’s probably fine but we’ll know.
Exactly. And tell her she was right to nudge you. See you after your shift.

social.t: A warehouse supervisor on shifts may struggle to attend appointments; he can usually swap shifts. If he later needs surgery on the thigh, heavy lifting and time off will need planning.
Men who “don’t want a fuss” often present late. The partner’s concern is a lever, not a nuisance.

legal.t: Not needed now. If investigation or treatment stops him working for more than 7 days, a fit note can be issued, including advice on adjusted or lighter duties.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): do not give false reassurance to please a patient; share uncertainty and a plan to resolve it.
A lump’s size, depth and mobility need an in-person examination. Document why imaging was requested before examination and arrange it promptly.

pitfalls.intro: The station hinges on one word in his opening — “bigger”. Candidates fail by reassuring a lipoma from the chair, or by offering to cut it out.

items.fail: Diagnosing a lipoma on video and advising watchful waiting.
items.why: NICE NG12: consider an urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks for an adult with an unexplained lump increasing in size.
items.fix: Request the ultrasound today and explain why.

items.fail: Offering minor surgery to remove it.
items.why: Unplanned excision of a sarcoma can compromise the specialist operation.
items.fix: Image first; excision only after specialist assessment.

items.fail: Not asking about depth, firmness, mobility and size.
items.why: These features, with growth, separate a likely lipoma from a lump that needs imaging.
items.fix: Ask on video, then examine and measure in person.

items.fail: Treating his partner’s concern as nagging and joining in the joke.
items.why: Collusion with minimisation loses the hidden agenda and Relating marks.
items.fix: “What do you think she’s worried about?” — then acknowledge his own worry.

items.fail: Using the word sarcoma or cancer abruptly, then moving on.
items.fix: Most likely harmless; a scan is how we know; here is the plan.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will contact you” and no fail-safe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Chase if no date in a week, named changes, GP review of the result.

Why you can’t call it a lipoma; urgent ultrasound within 2 weeks; no excision; in-person exam and measurement.

ice: Idea: “Just a fatty lump, like my mate’s”
Concern: it’s been growing, and that bothers him too
Expectation: to be told it’s harmless

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: An unexplained, enlarging, firm, deep lump on the right anterior thigh for 4 months in a 42-year-old man. Most likely benign, but it meets the NICE NG12 criterion for an urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks to assess for soft-tissue sarcoma.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Most lumps like this are fatty lumps. But yours is firm, deep and growing, and a few lumps like that are something else that can look the same from outside. A scan is the only way to tell them apart.”

management.reflectIce: “You said it’s been bugging you too. That’s a good instinct — and a scan is how we get you a proper answer instead of a guess.”
management.psychosocial: Fit appointments around shifts; involve his partner; frame the scan as precaution, not alarm.
sharedPlan: Urgent direct-access ultrasound requested today (within 2 weeks)
Face-to-face exam and measurement this week
Suspected cancer pathway referral if the scan is suspicious or uncertain
safetyNet: Ring if no scan date within a week
Contact sooner if rapid growth, pain or new lumps
GP reviews the result with him

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The station hinges on one word in his opening — “bigger”. Candidates fail by reassuring a lipoma from the chair, or by offering to cut it out.

items.fail: Diagnosing a lipoma on video and advising watchful waiting.
items.why: NICE NG12: consider an urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks for an adult with an unexplained lump increasing in size.
items.fix: Request the ultrasound today and explain why.

items.fail: Offering minor surgery to remove it.
items.why: Unplanned excision of a sarcoma can compromise the specialist operation.
items.fix: Image first; excision only after specialist assessment.

items.fail: Not asking about depth, firmness, mobility and size.
items.why: These features, with growth, separate a likely lipoma from a lump that needs imaging.
items.fix: Ask on video, then examine and measure in person.

items.fail: Treating his partner’s concern as nagging and joining in the joke.
items.why: Collusion with minimisation loses the hidden agenda and Relating marks.
items.fix: “What do you think she’s worried about?” — then acknowledge his own worry.

items.fail: Using the word sarcoma or cancer abruptly, then moving on.
items.fix: Most likely harmless; a scan is how we know; here is the plan.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will contact you” and no fail-safe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Chase if no date in a week, named changes, GP review of the result.
